title: Retriq programming documentation golden set - HTML language coverage

cases.question: Why does reading a state variable immediately after calling its setter still return the value from the current render?

expected.answer: Setting state requests another render; it does not mutate the state snapshot already captured by the running render or event handler.
keyFacts: A state setter requests a new render.
Each render receives a snapshot of state.
The current handler continues to observe the snapshot for its render.

approval.basis: Operational approval requested by the user after source/corpus verification; the user will independently confirm the case before final thesis reporting.

cases.question: How should a component increment the same state value three times in one event handler?

expected.answer: Pass an updater function to the setter three times, for example setNumber(n => n + 1), so React processes the queued updates in sequence.
keyFacts: Use the functional updater form.
React queues updater functions.
Each updater receives the result of the preceding queued updater.

evidence.section: Updating the same state multiple times before the next render

approval.basis: Operational approval requested by the user after source/corpus verification; the user will independently confirm the case before final thesis reporting.

cases.question: When is an Effect appropriate instead of deriving a value during rendering?

expected.answer: Use an Effect to synchronize with an external system. If no external system is involved and a value can be derived from props or state, calculate it during rendering.
keyFacts: Effects synchronize React components with external systems.
Derived values generally do not require an Effect.
Unnecessary Effects add extra render work and complexity.

cases.question: Why can ArrayStack resizing take linear time for one operation while still adding only constant amortized cost per update?

expected.answer: One resize copies n elements and costs O(n), but enough add or remove operations must occur between resizes. Across any sequence of m updates, the total resizing work is O(m), so the amortized resize cost per update is O(1).
keyFacts: A single resize allocates a new array and copies n elements, costing O(n).
At least roughly n/2 updates occur between consecutive resizes.
The total resizing time over m add/remove operations is O(m), giving O(1) amortized resizing cost.

approval.basis: Operational approval requested by the user after source/corpus verification; the user will independently confirm the case before final thesis reporting.

cases.question: What balance invariant does DualArrayDeque maintain, and why does its occasional O(n) rebalancing remain O(1) amortized per update?

expected.answer: Unless there are fewer than two elements, both front and back contain at least n/4 elements. Rebalancing moves Θ(n) elements, but at least roughly n/2 updates are required before another rebalance, so total balancing work over m updates is O(m).
keyFacts: Each side contains at least n/4 elements except for the very small case.
Rebalancing restores the two sides to floor(n/2) and ceil(n/2) elements.
A rebalance costs O(n), but sufficiently many updates separate rebalances, producing O(1) amortized balancing cost.

approval.basis: Operational approval requested by the user after source/corpus verification; the user will independently confirm the case before final thesis reporting.

cases.question: Under which assumptions does the LinearHashTable analysis obtain O(1) expected operation time?

expected.answer: The analysis assumes independent uniform hash values and maintains a load condition with at most half the table entries non-null. Under those assumptions, run lengths decrease exponentially and find, add, and remove take O(1) expected time before amortized resizing is included.
keyFacts: Hash values are assumed independent and uniformly distributed.
The table maintains q no greater than half the table length.
Run-length probability decreases exponentially, yielding O(1) expected find/add/remove time apart from resizing.
Resizing is handled separately with amortized analysis.

approval.basis: Operational approval requested by the user after source/corpus verification; the user will independently confirm the case before final thesis reporting.

cases.question: How does the correspondence with a 2-4 tree establish the height bound for a red-black tree?

expected.answer: Removing each red node and attaching its children to the black parent produces a 2-4 tree whose root-to-leaf paths have equal black height. A red-black path contains at most one red node between black nodes, so its length is at most twice the corresponding 2-4-tree height, giving height at most 2 log n.
keyFacts: Collapsing red nodes transforms the red-black tree into a 2-4 tree.
The black-height property gives equal root-to-leaf length in the transformed tree.
At most one of every two internal nodes on a red-black path is red.
The resulting red-black-tree height is at most 2 log n.

approval.basis: Operational approval requested by the user after source/corpus verification; the user will independently confirm the case before final thesis reporting.

cases.question: What are the main phases used by Java to determine whether a method is applicable during overload resolution?

expected.answer: Java first searches matching-arity methods applicable by strict invocation, then matching-arity methods by loose invocation only if phase 1 finds none, and finally variable-arity methods only if phase 2 finds none. Once a phase succeeds, the most specific applicable method is selected and later phases are not considered.
keyFacts: Phase 1 tests strict invocation.
Phase 2 tests loose invocation only if phase 1 finds no applicable method.
Phase 3 tests variable arity only if phase 2 finds none.
A successful phase selects the most specific method without proceeding to later phases.

cases.question: What atomicity guarantee does PostgreSQL provide for the statements enclosed by BEGIN and COMMIT?

Intermediate states are invisible to concurrent transactions.
COMMIT completes the transaction; ROLLBACK cancels updates made so far.
